sources.news_title: Auto industry slams Carney’s claim Canada can turn to China to replace U.S. automakers
sources.text:
Canadian automakers are dousing cold water on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s claim that Canada could turn to Chinese manufacturers if U.S. President Donald Trump chooses against preserving an integrated North American auto industry in ongoing trade negotiations.
Chinese automakers operating internationally typically use knock down kits that allow for limited assembly to bypass tariffs in host countries. Critics say these kits won’t come close to matching the economic footprint or create the same number of jobs of plants already operating in Canada.
Brian Kingston, president and CEO of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, said European countries that have lowered tariffs on Chinese cars have seen their auto industries decimated despite promises of Chinese companies relocating production.
He said the continent has lost 104,000 auto jobs in 2024 and 2025, and Germany’s auto industry lost 42,300 jobs in the first six months of 2026.
“There is no auto industry in Canada without US market access,” he posted on X.
Carney made the comments in Cambodia ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”
Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, said a Chinese company has never actually manufactured cars outside of that country and doubts that would happen with the industry currently producing millions of vehicles more than needed for their domestic market.
The International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers said China built around 35 million cars last year. But domestic sales dropped from 19.4 million in the first ten months of 2025 to 14.5 million units over the same period this year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
The industry association predicts that China exported around 7 to 8 million cars last year, and wants to bump that figure to 10 or 12 million this year to make up for falling domestic sales.
“The idea that the Chinese would invest in full assembly in Canada, while they haven’t done it anywhere else in the world, while they now have a a 13 million unit deficit for home consumption and an ability to make an extra 20 million at home is absurd,” he said.
Volpe pointed to the experience in Brazil as a warning sign for Canada. In 2025, the country gave China’s BYD tariff-free access for the company’s knock down kits for a six-month period. During that span, BYD was supposed to start the work towards beginning full production in Brazil.
That didn’t happen and Brazil suspended its exemption in February. But Brazil eventually relented and created a new exemption period that will last until the end of the year.
“BYD, the world’s biggest, fastest-growing [car company] has access to all kinds of Chinese capital has no real intention of [overseas] production, and we see what’s happened in Brazil,” Volpe said.
Asked by iPolitics about the industry’s criticism on Monday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Canada is fostering closer ties with China to support efforts to diversify trade away from the United States.
“This is part of our trade diversification strategy. It’s obviously normal and important to talk to your second largest trading partner, which happens to be the second largest economy in the world,” he said during a press event for an unrelated announcement.
“Prime Minister Carney will be seeing President Xi, and… I will let him reflect on the discussions they may have when they’re going to meet in Asia in the coming day.”
It’s expected that Canada will announce a new tariff agreement with China — potentially include new vehicles — tomorrow.

sources.news_title: Prime Minister Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
sources.text:
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”
Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada's auto workers and manufacturing assets.
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney's suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.
“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”
The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.
The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.
“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.
Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

sources.news_title: Canadian PM Mark Carney Threatens to Abandon U.S. Auto Industry for China
sources.text:
Far-left Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday that his country could turn to Chinese automakers for both vehicles and jobs if trade talks currently underway with the United States do not reach a satisfactory outcome.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market. That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions,” Carney said at a press conference in Cambodia.
Carney was in Cambodia for the Francophonie Summit, an annual meeting of about 90 member states who have cultural, linguistic, or historic ties to France. Cambodia, which has never hosted the summit before, was a French protectorate from 1863 to 1953.
Carney visited the Philippines on Saturday to conclude discussions on a free trade agreement, and he is due to meet with Chinese dictator Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China on Tuesday and Wednesday this week.
The Canadian prime minister denied he was using the threat of turning to China as leverage against the United States in trade negotiations.
“It’s not leverage. But action, reaction,” he said. “If [Canadian auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities. Canada is going to move forward either way.”
Carney said that if Canada does turn away from the United States to embrace Communist China, it will expect the Chinese to make substantial manufacturing investments on Canadian soil, using Canadian supply chains for parts and critical minerals.
“It’s not just about kit cars. There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved,” he insisted.
Canada imposed a 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) in 2024, along with a 25 percent tariff on Chinese steel and aluminum, following similar actions taken by the U.S. to protect its EV market against a flood of cheap Chinese imports. China retaliated with steep tariffs on Canadian canola oil, pork, seafood, and other agricultural products.
In January 2026, Canada broke with the U.S. policy approach by agreeing to dramatically reduce its tariffs on Chinese EVs in exchange for China lowering its retaliatory tariffs on Canadian food exports. Carney said the deal showed China has become a “more predictable” trade partner than the United States.
Carney’s loosened trade terms with China did not go over well in Ontario, the heart of the Canadian automobile industry. Ontario Prime Minister Doug Ford, furious that Carney did not consult him before opening the floodgates to Chinese imports, urged Canadians to “boycott the Chinese EV vehicles” and to “support companies that are building vehicles here.”
China’s actual penetration of the Canadian market turned out to be underwhelming, at least so far. The January 2026 agreement allowed Canada to import up to 49,000 Chinese EVs, but the actual number of imports was only about 16,200 by the end of September. A good deal of the quota was taken up by Teslas, produced at the American company’s “Gigafactory” in China.
Also, contrary to Carney’s confident predictions in January, China has yet to make any substantial investments in Canadian auto manufacturing. Four Chinese automakers met with Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly in June to discuss building their EVs in Canada, but nothing has come from those discussions yet, possibly because the Chinese companies are not eager to utilize Canada’s more expensive labor and supply chains.
China does seem interested in precisely the sort of “kit” manufacturing Carney promised to avoid. Last week, Doug Ford sent Carney a letter urging him not to allow “the introduction of Chinese-made knock-down kits” at the Stellantis Brampton auto assembly plant, which was recently purchased by Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel.
Roshel, in turn, said it plans to lease back 25 percent of the factory to original owner Stellantis — which would use the facility to assemble Chinese EVs from prefabricated kits that were manufactured in China. The proposal would wipe out hundreds, or even thousands, of jobs at the Brampton facility.
“We must remain aligned in our efforts to protect and expand Ontario and Canada’s automotive footprint. Fortifying Ontario and Canada’s industrial base, including a strong and growing automotive sector, is foundational to creating and realizing generational economic opportunities,” Ford wrote to Carney.
The Carney administration responded that it was “not considering any proposal to replace full vehicle manufacturing and assembly with Chinese-made kit cars,” and would continue to insist that Chinese investment in Canadian auto manufacturing “must use Canadian parts, Canadian labor, and a Canadian supply chain.”
As he was preparing to depart for Europe and Asia on Saturday, Carney said he had a “long, substantive conversation” with President Trump, and “we are making progress.”
“There is the possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal, but we’re not there yet,” he said.

sources.news_title: Carney opens the door to Chinese automakers as U.S. tariffs threaten North American auto integration
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada could seek investment from Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with President Donald Trump fail to preserve North America's integrated automotive industry, signaling that Ottawa is considering alternatives as U.S. tariffs disrupt cross-border manufacturing.
Speaking Monday in Cambodia ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, Carney said negotiations with Washington remained his priority but that Canada could explore partnerships with European, Japanese or Chinese manufacturers, according to The Associated Press.
"We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market," Carney said. "That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions."
Asked whether the prospect of Chinese investment was intended to pressure Washington, Carney replied: "It's not leverage. But action, reaction."
Carney emphasized that any Chinese investment would need to establish substantial manufacturing operations in Canada, comply with labor standards and develop domestic supply chains rather than simply assemble imported components.
Canada already reduced its tariff on Chinese electric vehicles from 100% to 6.1% under a January agreement, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
The comments followed Carney's announcement Saturday that Canada and the United States were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained. As The Associated Press also reported, Carney said any agreement must ensure Canada retains a viable automotive industry.
His government is also expanding partnerships beyond North America. On Sunday, Carney met Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Manila and announced up to $392 million in funding over four years for a tropical forest protection initiative led by Brazil, according to Bloomberg Línea.
Lula said the countries wanted to strengthen relations and potentially double bilateral trade. Both leaders also discussed reciprocal visits in 2027.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford has warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten domestic manufacturing jobs and complicate trade relations with Washington.
Carney's proposed alternative comes as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis maintain production networks spanning Canada, the United States and Mexico, with components frequently crossing borders before final assembly.

sources.text:
Canada could pursue ties with Chinese automakers if trade talks with the United States fail to secure the terms that Ottawa needs on the auto sector, Prime Minister Mark Carney says.
Carney made the comment while in Cambodia to attend an international gathering of French-speaking states and governments. His remarks come ahead of a scheduled meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be on the agenda.
Carney said while in the Philippines this weekend that any trade deal with U.S. President Donald Trump must preserve a viable auto industry in Canada. He told reporters on Nov. 16 that talks with Washington remain his priority, but the results could shape whether Canada explores alternatives with European, Chinese, or Japanese automakers.
Carney added that potential Chinese investment was not meant to act as leverage in negotiations with the White House but was “action” and “reaction” to them.
“It depends,” the prime minister said. “Look, great auto workers, important market, real assets ... if they’re not fully utilized in a North American context that provides other opportunities, Canada is going to move forward either way.”
He said Canada could also expand its cooperation with China in agriculture, energy, and financial services.

One source familiar with Canada-China trade negotiations said Beijing has been insisting on only lowering tariffs on a matching dollar-for-dollar basis, meaning it will agree to cut levies on an amount of Canadian imports as long as Ottawa lowers its tariffs for a commensurate amount of imports from China. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
A second source familiar with the Shenzhen talks said they anticipate additional tariff reduction announcements after the Carney-Xi meeting. They could not say if news would come immediately or later.
The Prime Minister offered no insight into whether China might roll back levies on agriculture or seafood.
He said Canada remains opposed to China shipping “kit cars,” or a set of parts to assemble a vehicle, which are delivered to be bolted together. Mr. Carney wants Chinese electric vehicle manufacturing in Canada to use Canadian parts, Canadian labour and critical minerals sourced in this country.
“The conditions for Chinese investment in Canada centre on standards for our workers. ... We aren’t talking about mere ‘kits,’” he said. “We are talking about full-scale vehicle manufacturing - actual factories and genuine processes, with supply chains that expand within Canada over time.”

Carney to tell Xi next week that foreigners shouldn’t interfere in Canadian affairs
The U.S. has a 100-per-cent tariff in place on Chinese-made electric vehicles. Canada, which imposed the same tariff in 2024 in tandem with the administration of Joe Biden, broke with the United States in January to scale back 100-per-cent tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles for a limited quota of 49,000 cars. In return, Beijing sharply reduced retaliatory levies on canola products and other agricultural shipments from Canada.

The four companies – BYD, Chery, Geely and Shanghai Launch Automotive Technology – had been examining possible investments in Canada. Ms. Joly said Shanghai Launch’s proposal included a partnership with British automaker Austin Motor Co.
The push to attract Chinese investment is part of an effort by the Carney government to save the Canadian auto industry as it faces an uncertain future because of protectionist U.S. trade policy.
Earlier this month, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu also met with BYD, Chery and Geely during a trip to China.

sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned that Canada could pursue partnerships with Chinese automobile manufacturers if negotiations with President Donald Trump fail to protect the country’s auto industry, signaling that Ottawa is prepared to look beyond the United States for investment and manufacturing opportunities.
Speaking to reporters this morning in Cambodia, Carney said preserving Canada’s participation in an integrated North American automobile market remains his preferred outcome. However, he made clear that continued American trade restrictions could force his government to explore alternatives involving manufacturers from China, Europe, and Japan.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”
His remarks came ahead of an anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, where cooperation in automobile manufacturing is expected to be discussed.
Carney had already stressed during a Saturday appearance in Manila that any agreement with Washington must ensure the continued viability of Canada’s automotive sector. While he described negotiations with the Trump administration as his first choice, he indicated that Canada would not remain dependent on the American market if those discussions failed to produce acceptable terms.
Asked whether the possibility of bringing Chinese automakers into Canada was intended to pressure Washington, Carney rejected that characterization.
“It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”
He said Canada’s skilled workforce and existing manufacturing facilities could attract investment from other international companies if American trade policies made cross-border production less attractive.
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
The dispute comes as President Trump continues pressing automobile manufacturers to shift production from Canada and Mexico into the United States. Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis maintain interconnected operations across all three countries, with components frequently crossing international borders several times during the production of a single vehicle.
Carney emphasized that any future Chinese investment would have to establish meaningful production operations inside Canada rather than merely use Canadian facilities to assemble imported components. He said potential agreements would need to include manufacturing plants, appropriate labor protections, and supply chains incorporating Canadian materials, including minerals essential to electric vehicle production.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
The possibility of expanded Chinese automobile manufacturing follows a trade arrangement reached by Ottawa and Beijing in January. Under that agreement, Canada lowered its tariff on a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles from 100% to 6.1%, initially permitting up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the quota scheduled to increase in subsequent years.
In return, China agreed to reduce tariffs on Canadian agricultural exports, including canola. Carney said the arrangement could eventually encourage Chinese manufacturers to establish operations in Canada and generate additional employment.
The agreement drew sharp opposition from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is home to much of Canada’s automobile industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into the Canadian market could threaten domestic manufacturing jobs and complicate Canada’s economic relationship with the United States.
Canada’s automotive industry has already been affected by the trade tensions. Ottawa recently threatened legal action against Stellantis after the company redirected planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois. The automaker also agreed to sell its inactive Canadian assembly facility, adding to concerns about the future of automobile manufacturing jobs in the country.
Carney nevertheless indicated that an agreement with Washington remains possible. He said Saturday that he had held extensive discussions with President Trump and senior American officials and that negotiations were advancing, although important disagreements had yet to be resolved.
The Canadian leader is expected to raise automobile investment during his upcoming meeting with Xi. The two countries have also been exploring broader economic cooperation involving agricultural exports, energy, financial services, and clean-energy technology, although no major new Chinese automobile manufacturing agreement in Canada has been announced.
